title: MCP 2026-07-28 Spec: Stateless Core & Enterprise Auth
content:
## Overview

On July 28, 2026, the Model Context Protocol steering group released the **MCP 2026-07-28 specification** — the most disruptive revision since MCP launched in November 2024. The headline change is that the protocol's core is now **stateless**: the same request can be answered by any server instance behind ordinary load-balanced HTTP infrastructure, instead of being pinned to the instance that started the session.

By this release, MCP's Tier 1 SDKs (TypeScript and Python) had each crossed 1 billion total downloads, with close to half a billion downloads a month combined — a sign of how central the protocol has become to agentic tooling since the [Tool Use & Agents](tool-use-and-agents) page was first written.

---

## Stateless Protocol Core

Previous MCP revisions treated a client-server connection as a stateful session, tracked via an `Mcp-Session-Id` header. The 2026-07-28 spec removes protocol-level sessions entirely. Every request now carries the context it needs to be answered independently, which means:

- Any server replica can answer any request — no sticky routing required
- Servers scale horizontally behind plain HTTP load balancers, the same way a REST API would
- Long-lived stateful behavior (e.g. long-running operations) moves out of the core protocol and into an explicit **extension** (see Tasks, below)

Alongside statelessness, the spec adds **Multi Round-Trip Requests** and **header-based routing**, and makes list results (tools, resources, prompts) cacheable — reducing the chattiness that stateful MCP sessions used to require.

---

## Authorization Hardening

**Dynamic Client Registration (DCR)** is now formally deprecated in favor of **CIMD** (Client ID Metadata Documents), a lighter-weight way for clients to declare their identity without a registration round-trip.

The **Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA)** extension was promoted to stable status. EMA lets organizations gate access to MCP servers through their existing identity provider (OAuth/OIDC), replacing the old pattern of a consent prompt per server with a zero-touch flow — a Claude Cowork or Claude Code user at an enterprise no longer approves each individual MCP connector by hand.

---

## Tasks Moves to an Extension

MCP's **Tasks** feature — used for tracking long-running operations that outlive a single request/response — has been pulled out of the protocol core and repackaged as a **versioned extension**, consistent with the new stateless design. Servers that need long-running-operation support opt into the Tasks extension explicitly rather than relying on core protocol behavior.

A companion **Apps** extension covers embedded UI — connectors that render interactive interface elements (not just text/JSON) inside a host like Claude Code or Claude.ai.

---

## Breaking Changes and Migration

The 2026-07-28 revision is **not backward compatible**. A server built against the 2026-07-28 spec may not work with an older client, and an old server won't understand the new stateless request shape. Teams running MCP servers in production need to:

1. Confirm which spec version each server and client declares
2. Migrate off `Mcp-Session-Id`-based session assumptions before adopting the new core
3. Move any long-running-operation logic onto the Tasks extension explicitly
4. Replace DCR-based client registration with CIMD where used

Claude Code and Claude Cowork have already been updated for 2026-07-28, including support for EMA's enterprise auth flow, connector observability, and private network tunnels for internal-only MCP servers.

---

## Why It Matters

The original MCP pitch was "build one server, use it from any client." Statelessness extends that pitch to infrastructure: an MCP server can now be deployed and scaled exactly like a normal stateless web service, rather than needing session-aware routing. Combined with EMA's centralized auth, this is aimed squarely at enterprise adoption — the friction points (scaling, per-server consent) that made large MCP deployments awkward are the ones this revision targets directly.
